text: 47 it should replace corticotropin or cor- ticosteroids as the treatment of choice,48-54 although others disagree.55,56 However, vigabatrin may offer the best first option in the treatment of infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis.54,57,58 In some countries, valproate, alone or with clonazepam and/or pyridoxine, has been tried for initial management of infantile spasms.59 Other second-line drugs include clobazam and topiramate;16 nitrazepam,16,48 felbamate,45,60 and lamotrigine45,60 have also been used. It is unclear to what extent treatment improves long-term outcome.38,46,58 Choice of antiepileptics in children. The use of antiepi- leptics in general in children has been reviewed.38,60-67 Again, appropriate treatment depends on seizure type, but there is a lack of evidence to support many therapeutic choices,62,67-69 in part because of the difficulties in under- taking studies in this population. In addition, children may be particularly susceptible to some adverse effects, includ- ing effects on behaviour, cognition, and development; be- havioural problems have been associated particularly with phenobarbital.67,70 Nonetheless the principles of pharma- cological management are similar to those in adults (above) although UK guidelines recommend that treat- ment should only be begun by a specialist.16 Dietary mod- ification (the ketogenic diet) may also be tried.67,71-74 Withdrawal of antiepileptic therapy. Concern over the potential adverse effects of antiepileptic therapy clearly makes withdrawal attractive in patients who achieve pro- longed seizure-free periods; however, the practical and so- cial consequences of seizure recurrence may be consider- able (for example, loss of driving licence and restricted employment prospects). The incidence of relapse after withdrawal has been variously estimated to range from 12% to over 60%.75,76 Many studies have been carried out in children; data in adults is more scanty and given the dif- ferences between the populations, extrapolation of results in children to adults may be invalid.75 A meta-analysis77 that included 25 studies and 5354 patients (children and adults) found the overall rate of relapse in seizure-free pa- tients after stopping antiepileptic therapy was 25% at 1 year and 29% at 2 years. There was a higher risk for re- lapse in adolescent- and adult-onset epilepsy compared with childhood-onset epilepsy. A more recent longitudinal population-based study78 following 148 patients long- term from the onset of epilepsy in childhood found that of 90 patients in whom antiepileptic therapy was stopped, 33 relapsed and although in most cases relapse took place within 3 years, in one case it occurred 28 years after with- drawal.
